# Measuring the Stars

Every star except the Sun is a point of light, even in the largest telescopes.
A faint one might be dim and near or brilliant and far. So: how far? Predict
first. Hold your thumb at arm's length and blink one eye, then the
other. Now hold it halfway to your face and blink again. Does it jump more,
less, or the same? Try it before you read on.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- compute a star's distance from its parallax;
- compare stars on the magnitude scale;
- order the spectral classes by temperature and place the Sun among them.

## Parallax {#parallax}

Your thumb jumps more when it is closer. That jump is **parallax**: the
apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when you change
your point of view.

For stars, the two points of view are Earth on opposite sides of its orbit,
six months apart. A nearby star shifts back and forth slightly against much
more distant stars. Half of the total shift is the **parallax angle**, p. The
nearer the star, the bigger p. Your eyes are the two ends of Earth's orbit;
your thumb is a very small star.

A star with a parallax of 1 arcsecond is, by definition, 1 **parsec** away
(parallax plus arcsecond). In general:

> d = 1 / p, with d in parsecs and p in arcseconds

One parsec is about 3.26 light-years, or about 206,000 times the Earth-Sun
distance. Half the parallax means twice the distance.

**Worked example.** Proxima Centauri, the nearest star after the Sun, has a
parallax of 0.77 arcseconds. So d = 1 / 0.77, about 1.3 parsecs, or about 4.2
light-years. Sanity check: the parallax is less than 1 arcsecond, so the
distance must be more than 1 parsec. It is.

Proxima has the biggest parallax of any star, still under one arcsecond. At
100 parsecs a star shifts 0.01 arcseconds, and the atmosphere blurs images by
about an arcsecond, so the best parallaxes come from space and reach a few
thousand parsecs. Parallax is the first rung of the **distance ladder**.

## Magnitudes {#magnitudes}

Brightness on the sky is measured in **magnitudes**, a scale from ancient
catalogs that called the brightest stars "first magnitude". Two warnings:

- **It runs backwards.** A smaller number means a brighter star, like golf
  scores. The brightest objects go negative: Sirius is about -1.5, the Sun
  about -26.7.
- **It is a ratio scale.** Five magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in
  brightness, so one magnitude is a factor of about 2.5.

**Apparent magnitude** is how bright a star looks from Earth. **Absolute
magnitude** is how bright it would look from a standard 10 parsecs, which
compares the stars' real power fairly. The Sun's absolute magnitude is about
4.8: from 10 parsecs it would be an ordinary naked-eye star.

## OBAFGKM {#spectral-classes}

In Orion, Betelgeuse is orange-red and Rigel blue-white: a temperature
difference. Like a stove burner, hot stars glow blue and cool ones red.

Astronomers sort stars into **spectral classes** by the dark absorption lines
in their spectra, whose pattern depends mainly on temperature:

| Class | Color | Surface temperature |
|---|---|---|
| O | blue | 30,000 K and up |
| B | blue-white | 10,000 to 30,000 K |
| A | white | 7,500 to 10,000 K |
| F | yellow-white | 6,000 to 7,500 K |
| G | yellow | 5,200 to 6,000 K |
| K | orange | 3,700 to 5,200 K |
| M | red | below about 3,700 K |

Each class splits into subclasses 0 to 9. The Sun is a **G2** star, about
5,800 K. Make up your own mnemonic for the order; the weirder, the better.

::: {.callout-important title="Common mistake"}
Farther stars do **not** show bigger parallax. Smaller parallax, farther star.
And keep p in arcseconds: plugging in degrees or arcminutes gives nonsense.
:::

## Self-check

```{=html}
<div class="quiz" data-answer="a">
  <div class="question">1. A star's parallax is 0.1 arcseconds. How far away is it?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> 10 parsecs, about 33 light-years</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> 0.1 parsecs</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> 1 parsec</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> 100 parsecs</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>a</strong>. d = 1 / 0.1 = 10 parsecs, and 10 x 3.26 is about 33 light-years.
  </div>
</div>

<div class="quiz" data-answer="d">
  <div class="question">2. Star A is magnitude 2 and star B is magnitude 7. Which is true?</div>
  <ul>
    <li data-choice="a"><label><strong>a.</strong> B is 5 times brighter than A</label></li>
    <li data-choice="b"><label><strong>b.</strong> B is 100 times brighter than A</label></li>
    <li data-choice="c"><label><strong>c.</strong> A is 5 times brighter than B</label></li>
    <li data-choice="d"><label><strong>d.</strong> A is 100 times brighter than B</label></li>
  </ul>
  <div class="explain">
    <strong>d</strong>. Smaller magnitude is brighter, and 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100.
  </div>
</div>
```

## Where this fits

Distance plus brightness gives luminosity; luminosity plus temperature builds
the next chapter's H-R diagram.
